exercises.prompt: Which of these lines are errors under `--strict` but compile when `strict` is off? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `function total(items) { return items.length; }`
options.feedback: Yes. `noImplicitAny` rejects the unannotated parameter instead of silently typing it `any`.

options.label: `try { f(); } catch (err) { console.log(err.message); }`
options.feedback: Yes. `useUnknownInCatchVariables` makes `err` `unknown`, so it must be narrowed first.

options.label: `const n: number = "5";`
options.feedback: Not yet. Assigning a string to a number is an error in every mode; strictness isn't needed for that.

hints: Three of these correspond to members of the strict family: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks and useUnknownInCatchVariables.
exercises.solution: (a), (b) and (c) are caught only with `strict` on, by `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks` and `useUnknownInCatchVariables` respectively; the lesson shows the actual messages. (d) is an ordinary type error that TypeScript reports whatever the settings.

exercises.prompt: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on, what is the type of `x` in `const arr: number[] = [1]; const x = arr[0];`?

feedback.message: Not yet. That's the type without the option. With it, every index read may be out of bounds as far as the compiler knows.

hints: The option assumes any index might be out of range.
exercises.solution: With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, indexing an array (or a record) adds `undefined` to the element type, because the compiler can't know whether the index exists: `number | undefined`. Assigning it to a `never` variable confirms it. Handle it with a check, a default (`?? 0`), or destructuring with a default.

exercises.prompt: Using the lesson's `median`, what does `console.log(median([2, 8, 4]), median([10, 20]))` print?
hints: Sort first. For an odd count, take the middle element; for an even count, average the two middle ones.
exercises.solution: `[2, 8, 4]` sorts to `[2, 4, 8]`; the length is odd, so the median is the middle element, 4. `[10, 20]` has even length, so the median is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. Output: `4 15`.

exercises.prompt: During a migration you must leave one known type error in place for now. Why do experienced teams write `// @ts-expect-error` with a reason, rather than `// @ts-ignore`?

options.label: `@ts-expect-error` itself becomes an error once there is no error to suppress, so it can't outlive the problem
options.feedback: Yes. When someone fixes the underlying issue, the compiler tells you to delete the comment.

options.label: `@ts-ignore` disables type checking for the whole file
options.feedback: Not yet. It suppresses errors on the next line only, just like `@ts-expect-error`; the difference is what happens when there is no error.

options.label: `@ts-expect-error` fixes the error automatically
options.feedback: Not yet. Neither comment fixes anything; they only suppress the report.

options.label: `@ts-ignore` is not supported any more
options.feedback: Not yet. It still works; it's just the less careful choice.

hints: What happens to each comment when the line below it no longer has an error?
exercises.solution: Both suppress errors on the following line. `@ts-expect-error` additionally reports an error ("Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive") if the next line has no error, so stale suppressions are found and removed. A short reason after it (`// @ts-expect-error: legacy API returns string ids until v3`) tells the next reader why it is there.

exercises.prompt: In the project, what message does `OrderSchema.parse({ id: "B-1", customer: { name: "Ife", tier: "member" }, lines: [] }, "orders[0]")` produce?
answers: orders[0].lines: expected an array of at least 1, got []
hints: `id` and `customer` are fine. What did `array(..., 1)` require of `lines`?
The path is built by `object` as `path.key`.
exercises.solution: `id` and `customer` pass. `lines` was declared with `array(object(...), 1)`, so an empty array fails, and the error carries the path `orders[0].lines`: `orders[0].lines: expected an array of at least 1, got []`.

exercises.prompt: In the project, a wholesale customer orders 20 units of one product at 500 cents each. What is `totalCents` on the invoice?

feedback.message: Not yet. 20 units reaches the wholesale minimum of 20, so the 12% bulk discount applies.
Not yet. That would be the member discount (5%). Wholesale gets 12% at 20 units or more.

hints: The wholesale discount is `{ kind: "bulk", minQty: 20, percent: 12 }`; is the minimum reached?
exercises.solution: The subtotal is 20 × 500 = 10000 cents. The quantity reaches the bulk minimum of 20, so the discount is 12% of 10000 = 1200 cents, and the total is **8800** cents. With 19 units, `discountCents` returns 0.

exercises.prompt: In a typed web application, where should run-time validation of incoming data happen?

options.label: Once, where the data enters (request handler, fetch result, file read), turning `unknown` into a precise type or a clear error
options.feedback: Yes. Parse at the boundary; inside, the types can be trusted.

options.label: Nowhere: the static types already guarantee the shape
options.feedback: Not yet. Types are erased; they say nothing about data that arrives while the program runs.

options.label: In every function, defensively, before using its arguments
options.feedback: Not yet. Re-checking everywhere clutters the code and duplicates what the types already guarantee once the edge has been validated.

options.label: Only in the database layer
options.feedback: Not yet. By then, unvalidated data has already passed through the rest of the program under false types.

hints: Recall "parse, don't validate" from lesson four.
exercises.solution: Validate once, at each boundary where untrusted data enters, with a schema that also produces the static type. After that point, functions accept precise types and need no defensive checks, because the compiler and the validator together guarantee them.
